subsection.paragraph: Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a point on the unit circle such that the radius $$\overline{OP}$$ forms an angle of $$\theta$$ radians with respect to the positive $$x$$ -axis (see Figure 7).

subsection.paragraph: We define the sine of the angle $$\theta$$ , written $$\sin\theta$$ , to be the $$y$$ -coordinate of $$P$$ . Similarly, the cosine of the angle $$\theta$$ , written $$\cos\theta$$ , is defined to be the $$x$$ -coordinate of $$P$$ . The other trigonometric functions, tangent, cosecant, secant, and cotangent of $$\theta$$ —written $$\tan\theta$$ , $$\csc\theta$$ , $$\sec\theta$$ , and $$\cot\theta$$ , respectively—are defined in terms of the sine and cosine functions.

subsection.paragraph: The next example illustrates how we find the trigonometric functions of an angle.

problem.paragraph: Find the sine, cosine, and tangent of $$\frac{5\pi}{4}$$ .

solution.paragraph: We first determine the reference angle for the given angle. As is indicated in Figure 11, the reference angle is $$\frac{5\pi}{4} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{4}$$ , or $$45^{{^\circ}}$$ . Since $$\sin 45^{{^\circ}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$$ and the sine is negative in Quadrant III, we conclude that $$\sin\frac{5\pi}{4} = \frac{- \sqrt{2}}{2}$$ . Similarly, since $$\cos 45^{{^\circ}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$$ and the cosine is negative in Quadrant III, we conclude that $$\cos\frac{5\pi}{4} = \frac{- \sqrt{2}}{2}$$ . Finally, since $$\tan 45^{{^\circ}} = 1$$ and the tangent is positive in Quadrant III, we conclude that $$\tan\frac{5\pi}{4} = 1$$ .

subsection.title: The Predator–Prey Population Model
subsection.paragraph: We will now look at a mathematical model of a phenomenon that exhibits cyclical behavior: the so-called predator–prey population model .

Next, recall that the sine and cosine functions oscillate between $$- 1$$ and $$+ 1$$ , so $$P_{1}(t)$$ is seen to oscillate between $$\left\lbrack {1000 + 100\left( {- 1} \right)} \right\rbrack$$ , or $$900$$ , and $$\left\lbrack {1000 + 100(1)} \right\rbrack$$ , or $$1100$$ , while $$P_{2}(t)$$ oscillates between $$\left\lbrack {20,000 + 4000\left( {- 1} \right)} \right\rbrack$$ , or $$16,000$$ , and $$\left\lbrack {20,000 + 4000(1)} \right\rbrack$$ , or $$24,000$$ . Finally, plotting a few points on each graph for, say, $$t = 0,2,3$$ , and so on, we obtain the graphs of the functions $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ as shown in Figure 20.

From the graphs, we see that at time $$t = 0$$ , the predator population stands at $$1000$$ owls. As it increases, the prey population decreases from $$24,000$$ mice at that instant of time. Eventually, this decrease in the food supply causes the predator population to decrease, which in turn causes an increase in the prey population. But as the prey population increases, resulting in an increase in food supply, the predator population once again increases. The cycle is complete and starts all over again.
